explain.say: Most bats hunt insects at night. Instead of relying on their eyes, they make short, very high-pitched calls, mostly too high for human ears.

explain.say: The call bounces off anything in front of the bat, a moth, a leaf or a tree, and a faint echo comes back. The bat's large ears are tuned to catch it.

explain.say: The time the echo takes tells the bat how far away the object is, and the difference between its two ears tells it which way. Changes in the echo even reveal the moth's size and movement.

faq.a: Echolocation means finding things by echoes. An animal makes a sound and listens for the echoes that bounce back, using the delay and direction to build a picture of its surroundings.
Mostly not. Most bat calls are between about 20 thousand and 120 thousand vibrations a second, above the top of human hearing. A bat detector shifts them down so we can hear them.
No, bats can see, and fruit bats have good eyesight. But in the dark, insect-eating bats rely mainly on echolocation because it works without light.
asks: Why do people say blind as a bat?

faq.q: How does a bat know how far away a moth is?
faq.a: Sound travels at a steady speed, so the longer the echo takes to return, the farther away the moth. The bat's brain measures delays of thousandths of a second.
asks: How does the bat measure distance?
How fast do bats work out distance?

faq.a: Yes. Dolphins and toothed whales use clicks underwater, and some cave birds, like oilbirds and swiftlets, use audible clicks to fly in dark caves.

facts: Most insect-eating bats call at frequencies between about 20,000 and 120,000 hertz, above the range of human hearing.
During the final attack on an insect, some bats call around 200 times per second, a sequence called the feeding buzz.
